subject: Culture
title: Seed Banks of the World
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Seed Banks of the World.

hook.text: Deep inside an Arctic mountain, a vault holds seeds from every nation. It's the doomsday backup.

buildup.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores over a million seed samples. It guards crop diversity against disaster.

discovery.text: Syria's seed bank was destroyed in war. Svalbard had the backup. Seeds came home to restart farming.

twist.text: 97% of vegetable varieties from 1900 are now extinct. We lost more food diversity than we saved.

climax.text: Seed banks aren't just science. They're cultural memory, preserving what entire civilizations ate.

punchline.text: A frozen seed is a civilization's insurance policy.

quiz.question: Where is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault located?

details.summary: Seed banks preserve agricultural biodiversity against catastrophe — the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway stores over one million seed samples in an Arctic mountain. These frozen libraries hold the genetic diversity needed to adapt crops to climate change, disease, and future food crises.
details.whyItMatters: Seed banks are humanity's insurance policy against agricultural catastrophe. The genetic diversity they preserve could save billions of lives if climate change devastates modern crop varieties.
takeaways: The Svalbard Vault stores over one million seed samples from worldwide
75% of crop genetic diversity has been lost since 1900
Syria's seed bank was evacuated during civil war to Lebanon

faq.question: How does the Svalbard Global Seed Vault work?
faq.answer: Located 400 feet inside an Arctic mountain in Norway, the vault stores duplicate seed samples from gene banks worldwide. Permafrost and thick rock maintain freezing temperatures even without power. Over 1,700 gene banks in 100+ countries have deposited seeds.

faq.question: Why is seed diversity important?
faq.answer: Modern agriculture relies on very few crop varieties, making food systems vulnerable. A single disease could wipe out a genetically uniform crop. Wild and heritage varieties carry genes for drought resistance, pest resistance, and nutritional value that modern varieties lack.
